findings.reason: The protected app-local driver declares the explicitly prohibited generic local `index` for the ValidWordAbbr object. The inert candidate preserves the complete class and app contract while using the genuine concept `validator`.

Apart from the prohibited driver name, the implementation is already the canonical design. Each abbreviation maps to its sole distinct word or None after a collision, so absent keys and exact-identity keys answer directly while duplicate dictionary entries remain harmless. The candidate changes no algorithmic behavior.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 288 and its Python design-class plus query-list adapter. The Reference preserves the abbreviation definition and three illustrative literals, the native uniqueness rule, the sole source operation trace and explanation, and all six constraints.

The protected app-local and native ValidWordAbbr classes remain structurally aligned, and the immutable native source remains tied to verified submission 2064311609. The app-only driver is the sole extra surface; the candidate renames only its object, is inert, and has not been submitted or represented as Accepted.

The previous benchmark made every word share one abbreviation, so a per-query dictionary scan found conflicts immediately and passed scaling. Legal 32/128/512-entry tiers now use six-letter dictionary keys and absent seven-letter query keys, forcing complete scans with a 16x total-character span. The candidate passes at -0.00 relative exponent and 1.03x largest ratio; the correct per-query scan fails only scaling at +1.18 and 190.08x.

The Approach now targets the candidate's validator driver, explains why identity rather than occurrence count matters, defines c and q exactly before the manifest bound, accounts for map storage, and covers short words, repeated words, ambiguous keys, and defensive empty input.

The hash-bound Premium Reference remains verified against authenticated source evidence, preserving the sole operation-trace example and full explanation, all six constraints, the exact short-word behavior, the uniqueness semantics, and the zero-visual structure.

coverage: The authenticated operation-trace example appears first with all five isUnique queries and their exact false, true, false, true, true results.

The previous sample row omitted the final cake query, an invented identity row was mislabeled as a sample, and the hidden collision row contained no colliding abbreviations; the replacement rows are visible and accurately classified.
The suite covers one- and two-letter identity abbreviations, three-letter numeric abbreviations, the maximum 20-letter word length, and matching endpoints with different middle counts.
Absent keys, exact sole identity, repeated identical dictionary entries, two distinct words sharing one key, and duplicates added after ambiguity exercise every uniqueness-map state transition.
Multiple abbreviation groups verify that ambiguity is isolated by key and that exact dictionary membership alone does not imply uniqueness when a different word shares the key.

Every authored result was independently evaluated from the literal rule that all dictionary words sharing a query abbreviation must equal the query; the protected source and inert candidate matched this oracle on 20,000 seeded randomized dictionary/query sets.
All 11 correctness cases are visible; the unchanged 32-, 128-, and 512-entry absent-key workloads remain hidden and performance-only in benchmark.json.
